title: A latent safety monitor flagged fewer harmful prompts than model refusals
summary: Across 15 language models and a held-out set of reworded prompts, one activation-based monitor flagged about 23% of harmful prompts at the same false-alarm rate as a string-matched refusal reference, which flagged about 32%. A later activation readout caught more, but analyses linked much of that gain to the model’s own refusal decision.
ai_technology: Latent Guard, linear and multilayer activation probes

source_review.scope: arXiv v1 front matter, aggregate §6 out-of-distribution reader comparison and matched false-alarm analysis

evidence.tested: The authors compared trained readers and string-matched model refusal at matched false alarm rates and tested how their scores tracked the models’ planned replies.
evidence.unknown: The comparison covers particular rewordings and learned monitors. It does not establish the limits of every activation-based safety monitor. Refusal wording can be missed by the reference detector; a sampled audit found only 13 of 135 replies labeled answered actually provided harmful assistance. Later-readout gains therefore do not all represent detection of genuine unsafe compliance.
evidence.ai_role: Learned latent readers classify prompts from instruction-tuned model activations and are checked against observed refusals and embedding models.
